commitResults.messageBody:
Billy both decided what to do and decided how to say it, mixing two jobs
that change for entirely different reasons. Ui now owns every word the
user sees and every line they type, so the rest of Billy can report what
happened without knowing how it appears.

Nothing outside Ui now mentions the divider lines, the banner or the
Scanner. Listing tasks builds its text and hands the whole block over
rather than printing line by line, which removed the last direct use of
System.out elsewhere. Reading input is Ui's job too, including trimming
the line, so no caller has to remember to do it.

Errors go through showError rather than show. The two print the same
thing today, but naming them apart makes the call sites honest about
what they are reporting and leaves one place to change if errors should
ever look different.

This is the first step towards A-MoreOOP and is a pure refactor: all 31
text UI cases pass unchanged, which is the point, since the user should
not be able to tell that anything moved.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a TaskList class to own the tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Billy held a bare ArrayList and reached into it directly, so the rules
about the list were spread across the commands that used it. Every
command taking a task number repeated the same two checks, and every one
of them did its own arithmetic to turn the number on screen into a
position in the list.

TaskList now owns the tasks and answers those questions itself. Its
methods take the number the user sees, counting from 1, so no caller
converts anything and the off-by-one this guards against cannot happen
outside the class. Whether a number names a real task is decided in one
place, by the object that actually knows.

What is left of parseTaskNumber is only the reading of a number from
text. The three failures a task number can have are unchanged and still
reported in the same order: text that is not a number, then an empty
list, then a number out of range.

Reading the tasks goes through an unmodifiable view, so listing and
searching can walk the list while adding and removing still have to go
through TaskList and cannot slip past its checks.

A pure refactor: all 31 text UI cases pass unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a Parser class for making sense of commands
commitResults.messageBody:
Over half of Billy was taken up with the shape of the typed language:
that the first word names the command, that a deadline puts /by before
its date, that a task is named by a number. None of that is what Billy
is for, and it meant a change to how commands are typed could be made in
the same file as a change to what they do.

Parser now owns that knowledge, including the separators and the usage
hints shown when a command is malformed. It hands back finished objects
rather than pieces of text: a Todo, a Deadline, an Event, a task number,
a day. Building the task while parsing is deliberate, since deciding
that "return book /by 2019-12-02" describes a deadline due that day is
exactly the making sense of a command that this class is named for, and
it means a half-built task never exists.

The result is that Billy's switch reads as a list of intentions, and its
remaining methods take values rather than text to pick apart: deleteTask
takes a number, listTasksOn takes a day.

ParsedCommand is a record because that is all it is, two values that
belong together and never change. Splitting the line once and passing
both halves on saves the caller taking it apart a second time.

A pure refactor: all 31 text UI cases pass unchanged. The order in which
a bad command is complained about is unchanged too, which matters,
because a task number is still read before the list is asked whether it
has such a task.

commitResults.messageTitle: Make Billy an object rather than a bag of static methods
commitResults.messageBody:
The four helpers now exist, but Billy still held them in static fields
and did all its work in static methods, which is to say it was a
namespace full of globals. Its state was reachable and replaceable from
anywhere, and nothing could be built twice.

A constructor now takes the file to work from and settles everything:
the Ui, the Storage and the tasks read from disk. All are final instance
fields, which recovers the immutability the task list lost when loading
had to replace it wholesale. run() then holds the conversation from
greeting to farewell, and main does nothing but build one and start it.

Loading in the constructor means the greeting would otherwise come after
the loading message, so what went wrong is remembered in a field and
reported by run() instead. A constructor's job is to leave the object
ready to work, not to write to the screen, so this separation is worth
the one field it costs.

describeTaskCount stays static because it uses no state at all, and a
method that needs no object should not pretend to.

Billy can now be built and run as two steps, over any file, more than
once, which is what makes the command handling testable without a
console.

A pure refactor: all 31 text UI cases pass unchanged, including the
order of the greeting and the loading message.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename the Command enum to CommandWord
commitResults.messageBody:
The stretch goal calls for an abstract Command class with a subclass per
command, and that name is currently taken by the enum of keywords. The
enum is worth keeping: it is the one place that knows which words Billy
accepts, and the list shown when a word is not recognised is built from
it, so the two can never disagree.

CommandWord says what it actually is, the word the user types, which
leaves Command free for the thing that is executed. A rename only: no
behaviour changes and all 31 text UI cases pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Turn each command into a class of its own
commitResults.messageBody:
Billy decided what every command meant in one switch, and held a method
per command beneath it. Adding a command meant another branch in a
method that only ever grows, and touching a file that has nothing to do
with the command being added.

Parser now returns a Command object that already holds what it needs,
and carrying it out is a matter of asking it to. Billy neither knows nor
cares which commands exist: the loop reads a line, parses it, executes
whatever comes back, and asks whether that was the last one. A new
command is a new class and a new line in Parser, and no existing command
is touched for it.

Adding is one class for all three kinds of task, because adding is the
same act whatever is added, and the task itself knows how to describe
and store itself. Marking and unmarking share a class too, differing
only in a boolean and the words reported. Exiting does nothing at all
when carried out; the farewell belongs to the end of the conversation,
not to the command, so that it appears whether the user said goodbye or
simply ran out of input.

The helpers a command needs are handed to execute rather than held as
fields, so a command carries only what makes it that command and can be
built without knowing which Billy will run it. Saving after a change is
shared by the abstract class, since it is the same act with the same
warning wherever the list changes.

The target's example prints the divider lines from the run loop. That is
not adopted here: Billy's Ui fences each message it prints, so a divider
per command would merge a save warning into the confirmation before it
and emit an empty pair for a command that says nothing. The polymorphic
dispatch is the point, and it is taken as given.

All 31 text UI cases pass. One caught a real regression while this was
being written, the farewell having been dropped when run was rewritten,
which is a fair advertisement for keeping them.
